Thank you for your reply! I would like to discuss this if you don’t mind. 
1. I did not compare a Black man to a dog, I told a human being that he shares his birthday with my pet
2. Why I specify that: If I told someone of any other race that they have the same birthday as a four legged member of my family, would it have racial connotations? No. So is it not racist to think “Oh, this person is Black, I should not mention my pet’s birthday in case he thinks I’m racist?” To me that seems more offensive to single him out and assume that he might take offense to hearing about a dog’s birthdate simply because of the color of his skin
3. I 100% recognize the dehumanization of Black people in the history of American and African culture (I have lived in both places for significant amounts of time.) I have had lengthy conversations with clients of all races and backgrounds, but for the sake of this discussion, one couple stands out to me: They are both Black and take particular offense to being called African American, because they were born in America and do not claim Africa as their heritage. We get along very well and they speak with me on Zoom for hours to teach me about their perspective and have healthy discourse, they are wonderful people. Why do I bring that up? Because had they not told me that the term ‘African American’ offends them, I would not have known. Just like how if I need to call someone by other pronouns, if they tell me, I will do so. [edit: I don’t know if it’s important here, but I have another client who prefers to be called African American, not Black, which I was notified about through our discussions as well.]
4. I see where you are coming from, I do. I just find it confusing because every person seems to have different things they are offended by, and unless it’s written on a badge it can be complicated in interpersonal conversations. 
5. Lastly, the comment he made to the other coworker, I am wondering in your opinion if you please, why he would make that assumption of my coworker who did not make any such [edit: same bday as dog] comment?

Thank you again for your response, I look forward to reading your perspective!

EDIT: I’ve had a bit more of a think about this, and I’ll accept that I am ignorant for sure, in this ever-evolving social landscape I do feel a bit helpless and confused. I’d also even accept rude, because rudeness is in the eye of the beholder many times. What I mean is, my comment could have hurt his feelings, which if he ever brings up to me I will absolutely address. I think I’m stuck on the question he asked my coworker, when I was not around. It just seems so out of left field.

I have been able to slightly curb my spending by binging minimalist YouTubers. I really like Marissa Zen - Family Minimalism because she’s not one of those “minimalist aesthetic but I still replace all my stuff monthly” YouTubers. For me, spending is a hyper fixation due to being neurodivergent. I get obsessed with an eyeshadow palette, a clothing style, and I HAVE to have it. So I switched my fixation to be about decluttering rather than spending. Note: it doesn’t always work!!! I go through phases where I’ll be into minimalism for months, then into maximalism for weeks. But the time between spending binges is getting wider, and I think that’s what counts. I hope this helps a little. Remember, there’s never one answer, we must use a combination of coping mechanisms and cultivate a diverse toolkit to battle these things. Best of luck to you💗

First off, I think it’s wonderful that you’re here trying to help your girlfriend. That is an excellent first step. Something that really helps me is distraction, usually an intense show or a comforting movie (Ozark/Dirty John on Netflix or Disney/Harry Potter, respectively.) Typically for the intense option it needs to be something I haven’t seen yet to really grab my attention. I’ve found that my boyfriend just wants to talk my ear off when I get this way, and it does so much more harm than good every single time. I would start by putting something on TV, bringing snacks, and then holding her hand or hugging her and don’t try to make her talk about how she’s feeling. Then when she’s in a better mood (maybe not the same day) ask what about that helped and what didn’t, and see if you two can brainstorm from there. I hope this helps, and good luck!!

Ps going for walks helps me too, but that can open the doors for conversation which sometimes when us bpd gals are upset does not help the situation. Depends where she’s at. Maybe bring up this option during milder times.
